EDS AI Workflow (Eitri Agentic Dev Workflow)

Path to production

Code changes pass through four pipeline stages on their way to production. Each stage widens the scope of the checks, from the developer’s staged change at commit time to the whole codebase at QA entry and before release. The same checks are reused at each scope, so enforcement stays consistent without duplicate tooling.

The path starts where the developer harness closeout ends and finishes with the consolidated report for the Tech Lead’s release sign-off.

AIHow AI can help in this chapter

  • Explain review findings
  • Check generated documents
  • Prepare readiness evidence

Follow the four pipeline stages

A commit triggers checks on the staged change only. A merge request (MR) to the Dev branch generates documentation for the changed files. An MR to the QA branch runs full-codebase scans and document generators. Promoting a release candidate runs every readiness gate again on the full codebase and produces one report for the Tech Lead.

The pipeline has four stages, numbered 4.1 to 4.4 below.

Pipeline stages, triggers, checks, scope and blocking behaviour
StageTriggerWhat runsScopeBlocking
4.1 Pre-commitEach commit, through an automatic hookThe quality and compliance reviews from the build loop, including the IM8 reviewStaged changeBlocks the commit on Critical or High findings
4.2 Merge to DevMR targeting the Dev branchAPI documentation generationChanged files in the MRDoes not block
4.3 Merge to QAMR targeting the QA branchSecurity scans, the authorisation matrix and the technical architecture documentFull codebaseScans block on Critical or High findings; generated documents do not block
4.4 Pre-productionRelease candidate promotionEvery readiness gate, in one runFull codebaseBlocks the release on any gate failure

4.1 Check each commit

An automatic hook reviews the staged change whenever a developer commits. It is the same quality and compliance gate used inside the build loop, scoped to the staged change for fast feedback. It runs in parallel the review against coding standards and the specification, Semgrep static analysis, the IM8 security review, the thermo-nuclear maintainability review and the framework reviews.

When the hook runs, a Critical or High finding blocks the commit and its results are written to one consolidated report. Local hooks can be bypassed. Required release controls should also be enforced in the shared pipeline; follow the applicable exception process and retain the reason and follow-up evidence for any authorised bypass.

The IM8 review checks application technical controls such as input validation, authentication, secrets management, session management and audit logging.

AIHow AI can help

An AI reviewer can help relate a finding to the staged code and propose a correction. Give it the actual report and applicable rule. The developer checks the location and reasoning, reruns the original checks and retains the new results; scanners and pipeline rules determine their own pass or fail states.

4.2 Document changes when merging to Dev

An MR to the Dev branch generates API documentation for the changed files only, from comments in the code, so reviewers can see quickly what changed in each interface. This stage does not block the merge. Documentation for the full codebase is generated at pre-production.

4.3 Scan the full codebase when merging to QA

An MR to the QA branch runs full-codebase security scans and document generators. Their outputs support threat and risk analysis and technical documentation sign-off.

Checks at the merge to QA
CheckWhat it providesBlocking
IM8 reviewA finding for each IM8 application technical control, with the code locationBlocks on Critical or High
Authorisation matrixA map of each role to the endpoints and resources it can reach, with endpoints that lack authorisation flagged as potential gapsDoes not block
Technical architecture documentSystem overview, module catalogue, technology decisions, database design and a dependency inventory with licencesDoes not block
Dependency vulnerability scanKnown vulnerabilities (CVEs) by severity for each package, with upgrade guidance for Critical and High findingsBlocks on Critical or High CVEs
Semgrep static analysisFindings such as injection, weak cryptography, hard-coded secrets and unsafe input handlingBlocks on Critical or High

All outputs are point-in-time and are regenerated after codebase or dependency changes.

AIHow AI can help

When AI assists with an authorisation matrix or architecture document, ground it in the current code and interface definitions. Engineers check role-to-endpoint mappings and dependencies against the implementation and retain the reviewed documents. Generated documentation does not replace the configured security scans.

4.4 Confirm pre-production readiness

Before a release candidate is promoted, one skill runs every readiness gate in sequence on the full codebase and writes one sign-off report for the Tech Lead. Any gate can also be rerun on its own.

  1. Generate API documentation.
  2. Generate the authorisation matrix.
  3. Produce the threat model for review, using OWASP Threat Dragon.
  4. Generate the technical architecture document, including the dependency vulnerability scan.
  5. Check the full codebase against IM8 controls.
  6. Check observability readiness through a logging review.
  7. Audit secrets and configuration with Semgrep.
  8. Write the consolidated sign-off report for the Tech Lead’s review.

Most of these checks also ran at earlier stages; here they run again against the release candidate to provide point-in-time evidence for the Tech Lead. Passing them does not establish that all threats, vulnerabilities or applicable controls have been covered. Two are pre-production only:

  • Threat modelling: models the system as data-flow diagrams and identifies threats with the STRIDE method, which groups security threats into six categories, adding LINDDUN, a privacy threat modelling framework, for privacy-sensitive features. Each threat is recorded as mitigated, not applicable or open, with a mitigation for every open item. The model is kept in version control and updated when the architecture changes.
  • Observability: checks that logging is ready for production, including log levels, exception logging, leakage of sensitive or personal data, and correlation identifiers that follow a request across asynchronous work.

Note

The pre-production report covers IM8 controls in the code. ARC controls are assessed earlier, against the TRD, at the compliance audit in Step 8. Keep the TRD assessment and code-check results together for the release review.

AIHow AI can help

AI can help organise current gate outputs into a draft readiness summary with links to the reports and unresolved findings. The Tech Lead checks that the evidence matches the release candidate and every required result is present, then records the release decision through the existing process.

Plan what happens after readiness

The pipeline gates establish readiness for release, not the rollout itself. Plan limited exposure, observation and recovery, and feed production evidence back into the next PRD, using the Release and observe and Learn stages in Product implementation.

Definition of done for the pipeline and pre-production

Pipeline gates are done (stages 4.1–4.3) when

  • Pre-commit: the quality and compliance review, including the IM8 review, reports no Critical or High findings on the staged change.
  • Merge to Dev: API documentation is generated for the changed files.
  • Merge to QA: the IM8 review, the dependency vulnerability scan and Semgrep report no Critical or High findings on the full codebase.
  • Merge to QA: the authorisation matrix and the technical architecture document are generated.

Pre-production is done (stage 4.4) when

  • API documentation and the technical architecture document are generated.
  • The authorisation matrix is generated and reviewed, including any endpoints flagged as unprotected.
  • The threat model is reviewed and all findings are triaged.
  • No Critical or High CVEs remain unmitigated.
  • Full-codebase IM8 compliance and observability readiness are confirmed.
  • The secrets and configuration audit reports no critical security findings.
  • The consolidated report is approved by the Tech Lead.

Next step: check which of these stages your pipeline already enforces, and agree with your platform team how the missing ones will be added. To change what each stage checks against, add your team’s context.

Confirm the secrets/configuration audit’s blocking severity with the workflow owner: this local definition mentions critical findings, while earlier pipeline checks block Critical or High. Do not assume those thresholds are equivalent. Local workflow revision and verification limits.

Eitri status and version: verify installed revisions and enforced controls.

  2. SG Tech Stack. Eitri AI coding workflow — self-paced training. Live, version-dependent public training, not certification of an installed harness. The public course contains mixed revisions. This guide retains the local 19-step view. Confirm the applicable harness revision and release controls with the workflow owner before transferring commands or relying on a gate. Used in guided workflow context. See current skills lesson.
  3. Semgrep. Semgrep — static security analysis. Underlying scanner reference, not verification of the rules, severity mapping or blocking behaviour configured in the EDS harness. Used in pre-commit review, QA scans, secrets and configuration audit.
  4. Singapore Government. Instruction Manual 8 (IM8) — ICT and Smart Systems policy framework. Policy reference, not evidence of the installed application-security checklist or its enforcement. Packaged checks are a scoped selection, not a total for the entire framework; confirm the applicable policy and policy-pack versions with their owners. Used in staged-change review, full-codebase review, pre-production code checks.
  5. Cursor. Thermo-nuclear code quality review — skill instructions. Live main-branch skill reference for maintainability review. The EDS wrapper and installed upstream revision require confirmation; review findings are not proof of correctness. Used in maintainability review.
  6. OWASP. Threat Dragon — threat modelling. Underlying tool for data-flow diagrams and threat-model artefacts. Generated models still need review; the tool reference does not establish EDS readiness gates. Used in threat modelling.
  7. Microsoft Learn. Threat Modeling Tool threats — STRIDE. Framework reference for the six security-threat categories used in the documented threat-modelling gate, not evidence that the model is complete or enforced. Used in security threat categories.
  8. LINDDUN project. LINDDUN — privacy threat modelling. Privacy framework used for privacy-sensitive features in the documented workflow; applicability and mitigation decisions remain subject to review. Used in privacy threats.
  9. GovTech. Agentic Risk & Capability Framework (ARC). Governance framework underlying the documented TRD audit. Checklist coverage and applicable versions require owner confirmation; a document assessment does not establish executable or runtime enforcement. Used in the distinction between TRD assessment and code checks.
